description: The control environment criteria begin with demonstrated commitment to integrity and ethical values. A documented, acknowledged code of conduct is the artifact auditors look for as evidence that expectations were set and accepted rather than assumed.
implementation_guidance:
Publish a code of conduct covering ethical behaviour, acceptable use, conflicts of interest and confidentiality.
Require every employee and contractor to acknowledge it at hire and annually thereafter.
Track acknowledgement centrally so completion can be evidenced per person.
Route non-completion through the disciplinary process rather than leaving it open.
name: Code of conduct and ethics policy

evidence.name: Approved code of conduct
Acknowledgement from every member of staff
Record of breaches and the action taken

description: The criteria require that individuals are held accountable for their control responsibilities. A documented and consistently applied disciplinary process is what makes policy enforceable rather than advisory.
implementation_guidance:
Define the disciplinary process in policy, including the range of sanctions and who decides them.
Reference it in the code of conduct that staff acknowledge, so the consequence is known in advance.
Apply it consistently when violations occur, as inconsistent enforcement undermines the control.
Retain records of the decision and its basis, handled confidentially through HR.
name: Documented disciplinary process

evidence.name: Disciplinary procedure
Sample of cases showing the procedure was applied

description: The criteria require that reporting lines and authorities are established. An accurate structure shows that security duties sit with real roles holding the standing to carry them out, rather than being distributed informally.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a current organizational chart showing reporting lines.
Maintain role descriptions that state the security responsibilities attached to each role.
Review both at least annually and after any reorganization.
Confirm security roles retain a reporting line independent enough to raise issues without conflict of interest.
name: Organizational structure and reporting lines

evidence.name: Current organization chart with reporting lines
Role descriptions for security and compliance roles
Minutes where the board or leadership reviewed the structure

description: A security programme without a single accountable owner fragments across teams and stalls at decisions nobody is empowered to make. A formally designated officer gives the programme an escalation point and gives the auditor a name.
implementation_guidance:
Formally designate a security officer or equivalent lead in policy or by board resolution.
Document the role's authority, budget and escalation path, and its reporting line to the oversight body.
Name a deputy so accountability survives absence and turnover.
Review the designation whenever the role changes hands.
name: Designated security officer

evidence.name: Appointment or role charter naming the security officer
Report or briefing from the security officer to leadership

description: SOC 2 expects a governing body independent of management to oversee the security programme. Without a documented record of that oversight there is no evidence that leadership exercised the accountability the criteria require.
implementation_guidance:
Put security posture, material incidents, risk assessment results and remediation progress on the board or oversight-body agenda at least annually, and quarterly where practical.
Provide a written pack rather than a verbal update, so the information given to the body is itself evidence.
Retain agendas, packs and minutes recording what was discussed and decided.
Record any resourcing or risk-acceptance decisions the body makes.
name: Board / executive security oversight

evidence.name: Charter of the board or executive committee covering security oversight
Minutes showing security was discussed and challenged
Record of who sits on the body and their independence

description: Monitoring only closes the loop when results reach people who can allocate resources. A recurring management review is where control health, findings and risk are considered together, and where remediation is prioritized against everything else competing for effort.
implementation_guidance:
Hold a management review at least quarterly, covering control health, open findings, incidents, risk register changes and remediation progress.
Record attendees, decisions, resource commitments and actions with named owners.
Carry unresolved actions forward to the next review rather than closing them silently.
Escalate items that have missed two consecutive reviews to the oversight body.
name: Periodic management review of security

evidence.name: Management review agenda and minutes
Actions raised in the review and their closure

description: Accountability that is not assigned is not accountability. The criteria require authorities and responsibilities to be defined so individuals know what they own, and so a failing control has a name attached to it.
implementation_guidance:
Map every control to a named owner, and record the authority that owner holds to act.
Review the mapping at least annually and whenever someone changes role or leaves.
Reassign ownership as part of offboarding so no control is left orphaned.
Keep ownership at the level of a person, not a team inbox, for controls that require judgement.
name: Assigned control ownership (RACI)

evidence.name: Control ownership register
Updated ownership when roles change

description: Risks can only be identified against objectives that have been stated. The system description defines the boundary, the commitments made to customers and the requirements that follow, and it anchors both the risk assessment and the audit scope.
implementation_guidance:
Document the system boundary, covering infrastructure, software, people, procedures and data.
State the service commitments and system requirements made to customers, as those are what the audit tests against.
Describe subservice organizations and state clearly which controls are carved out.
Review annually and on material change, and reconcile the description against what is actually deployed.
name: System description and service commitments

evidence.name: System description covering boundary, services, infrastructure, people and data
Service commitments and system requirements shared with customers

description: The risk assessment is the foundation the rest of the programme rests on: it determines which controls are needed and where effort is justified. Controls selected without one are difficult to defend as sufficient.
implementation_guidance:
Perform a formal risk assessment at least annually, and on significant change to the business or environment.
Identify threats to defined objectives, including fraud and third-party risk.
Score likelihood and impact against a documented scale, and record both inherent and residual risk.
Retain the methodology so results are reproducible and comparable year over year.
name: Annual risk assessment

evidence.name: Risk assessment report with method and scope
Management sign off on the assessment

description: A risk that is identified but not tracked is not managed. The register is the operational record showing each risk has an owner, a rating and a decision, and it is what an auditor traces from assessment through to control.
implementation_guidance:
Capture risk description, category, owner, inherent rating, mitigating controls, residual rating and treatment decision of accept, mitigate, transfer or avoid.
Review the register at each management review and record rating changes with dates.
Require named sign-off at an appropriate level for any accepted risk.
Link each risk to the controls that mitigate it so coverage can be verified.
name: Risk register with treatment decisions

evidence.name: Risk register with owners, ratings and treatment decisions
Approval of each accepted risk

description: A treatment decision only reduces risk once it is executed. The treatment plan turns intent into scheduled, owned work, and it is the evidence that residual risk ratings reflect reality rather than aspiration.
implementation_guidance:
For each risk being mitigated, record the specific treatment actions, the accountable owner, the target date and the expected residual rating.
Track actions to closure with evidence rather than status updates alone.
Re-rate the risk only once the treatment is demonstrably in place.
Report overdue treatment actions at management review.
name: Risk treatment plan

evidence.name: Treatment plan with owners and due dates
Evidence that treatments were completed

description: SOC 2 requires fraud risk, including insider misuse and management override, to be considered explicitly in the risk assessment. Teams routinely assess external threats and omit this, which is a recurring exception.
implementation_guidance:
Include a fraud and insider-threat section in the annual risk assessment, covering incentive, opportunity and rationalization.
Consider management override of controls specifically, as it is the scenario most often left out.
Map identified fraud risks to mitigations such as least privilege, segregation of duties, logging and independent review.
Record the conclusion even where the assessed risk is low.
name: Fraud and insider-threat consideration

evidence.name: Fraud risk assessment covering insider misuse and management override
Actions taken on the fraud risks found

description: Risk assessed once a year goes stale as soon as the environment changes. A new subprocessor, a new data type or a major architectural shift can introduce risk that the annual cycle will not surface for months.
implementation_guidance:
Define the triggers that force an out-of-cycle risk review: onboarding a subprocessor that touches customer data, a major architecture or hosting change, a new data type or jurisdiction, or significant organizational change.
Require the triggered review before the change goes live, not after.
Document each review, its conclusion and any new risks added to the register.
Review the trigger list annually so it keeps pace with the business.
name: Change-triggered risk review

evidence.name: Procedure listing what triggers a risk review
Risk reviews done after significant changes

description: Controls exist to mitigate identified risks. Without an explicit mapping it cannot be shown that every material risk is addressed, nor can it be known which risks a failing control leaves exposed.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a mapping from each risk in the register to the controls that mitigate it.
Flag any risk with no mitigating control, and any control that maps to no risk.
Require a documented acceptance decision, signed by the risk owner, for risks deliberately left unmitigated.
Revisit the mapping whenever a control is disabled or a new risk is added.
name: Risk-to-control mapping

evidence.name: Risks linked to the controls that mitigate them

description: Application controls rest on general technology controls. Where access, change management or operations are weak on any system in the footprint, every control depending on that system inherits the weakness.
implementation_guidance:
Inventory the full technology footprint, including systems introduced through acquisition or adopted informally.
Confirm each system is covered by access control, change management and operations controls.
Document any system deliberately out of scope, with the rationale and any compensating controls.
Reconcile the inventory against billing and identity-provider records to find systems nobody registered.
name: IT general controls coverage

evidence.name: Inventory of in scope systems and the general controls over each
Review that every system is covered by access, change and operations controls

description: Policies are how control expectations are deployed consistently across the organization. A gap in the policy set marks an area where practice is undefined and therefore cannot be shown to operate consistently.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain the core policy set: information security, access control, change management, incident response, business continuity and disaster recovery, vendor management, data handling, acceptable use and secure development.
Ensure each policy is formally approved, versioned and dated.
Map each policy to the criteria it supports so coverage gaps are visible.
Make the current set available to all staff at a known location.
name: Security policy suite

evidence.name: Published security policies covering each required topic
Approval record for each policy

description: Policies that no longer describe how the organization actually operates are among the most common audit exceptions. An annual review forces each policy to be read against current practice, re-approved by an accountable owner, and corrected where the two have drifted apart.
implementation_guidance:
Review every policy at least annually, and sooner after a material change to the business or environment.
Record the reviewer, the review date and the outcome, even where the outcome is no change.
Re-approve through the documented approval path rather than editing in place.
Retain superseded versions so the version history can be traced at audit.
name: Annual policy review

evidence.name: Review and re approval record for each policy

description: A Type II opinion covers a period, not a date. Controls must therefore be shown to operate throughout that period, which point-in-time checks cannot demonstrate. Ongoing evaluation is what moves a control from designed to operating effectively.
implementation_guidance:
Run automated checks continuously against connected systems and retain each result with its timestamp, so the operating history is preserved.
Route failures to the named control owner with a remediation SLA.
Review recurring failures for design weakness instead of closing each occurrence individually.
Record periods where monitoring itself was unavailable, as that is a gap in the operating evidence.
name: Continuous control monitoring

evidence.name: Control test results across the observation period
Exceptions found by monitoring and how they were resolved

description: A penetration test is an adversarial evaluation of controls as they actually run rather than as they are documented. It surfaces exploitable weaknesses that scanning and self-assessment consistently miss.
implementation_guidance:
Commission an independent penetration test at least annually, and after major architectural change.
Scope it to cover internet-facing applications and infrastructure, and state any exclusions in the report.
Track findings to remediation against a severity-based SLA.
Obtain retest confirmation for high and critical findings, and retain the report and attestation letter.
name: Annual penetration test

evidence.name: Penetration test report from an independent tester
Remediation of findings, with retest evidence

description: An internal assessment before the audit window converts surprises into planned work. It provides the independent evaluation the monitoring criteria expect and gives management time to remediate before an exception reaches the opinion.
implementation_guidance:
Perform an internal control review or readiness assessment at least annually and ahead of the audit window.
Use a reviewer independent of the controls being reviewed wherever the team is large enough to allow it.
Document scope, method, evidence examined and findings, not just a conclusion.
Route findings into deficiency tracking so remediation is managed like any other finding.
name: Internal audit / readiness assessment

evidence.name: Internal audit or readiness assessment report
Remediation plan for the gaps found

description: Identifying a deficiency is only half the control; the criteria require that deficiencies are communicated to those responsible and corrected. Untracked findings recur, and a pattern of repeat findings is itself an audit exception.
implementation_guidance:
Record every finding from audits, tests, monitoring and incidents in one tracker with an owner, severity, root cause and due date.
Drive due dates from a severity-based SLA rather than negotiating each one.
Require closure evidence rather than self-attestation before a finding is closed.
Escalate items that age past their SLA to management review.
name: Deficiency remediation tracking

evidence.name: Log of control deficiencies with owner, due date and closure
Communication of deficiencies to the people responsible

description: Obligations arrive from contracts, regulation and certification commitments, and each changes independently of the others. A single register turns a scattered set of promises into a managed list, so an obligation is not discovered only when it has been breached.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a register of every applicable legal, regulatory and contractual obligation with its source, owner and review date.
Map each obligation to the controls that satisfy it, so coverage gaps are visible.
Review the register at least annually and whenever entering a new market or signing commitments with new requirements.
Assign a named owner to each obligation rather than to the register as a whole.
name: Compliance obligations register

evidence.name: Register of contractual, regulatory and certification obligations
Review of the register for new obligations

description: Policies only influence behaviour if staff can find them and know they apply. Acknowledgement is the evidence that expectations were communicated, which the communication criteria require.
implementation_guidance:
Publish the current policy set where all staff can access it without needing to ask.
Track acknowledgement at hire and on material change, per person and per policy.
Communicate changes actively rather than relying on staff to notice a new version.
Follow up outstanding acknowledgements, escalating persistent non-completion.
name: Internal policy portal

evidence.name: Policy portal showing current policies available to staff
Staff acknowledgement of current policies

description: Staff and customers often notice incidents before monitoring does. A known, low-friction reporting channel is what converts that observation into an alert instead of a private concern.
implementation_guidance:
Operate a dedicated reporting channel, such as a security alias or a monitored chat channel.
Communicate it at onboarding, in training and in the incident-response plan.
Monitor it during defined hours and route reports into the triage process.
Encourage reporting of suspicion rather than certainty, and respond without blame so people keep reporting.
name: Security incident reporting channel

evidence.name: Published reporting channel for staff and customers
Sample of reports received and how they were handled

description: A confidential reporting path allows misconduct to be raised where the normal management line is part of the concern. Its existence supports the integrity and accountability criteria directly.
implementation_guidance:
Provide a confidential and, where practical, anonymous reporting mechanism.
Document how reports are received, investigated and escalated, and who is excluded from handling a report about themselves.
Communicate the mechanism to all staff and state the prohibition on retaliation.
Record reports and their handling confidentially, and report volume to the oversight body.
name: Whistleblower / ethics reporting mechanism

evidence.name: Description of the confidential reporting mechanism
Anonymized log of reports received and outcomes

description: Customers are entitled to know the security, availability and privacy commitments being made to them. Those published commitments are also what the audit tests the system against, so they must match reality.
implementation_guidance:
Publish terms of service, service level commitments, a security or trust page and a privacy notice.
Ensure published commitments match what the controls actually deliver, as an overstated commitment creates an exception.
Review published material at least annually and after material change to the service.
Record approval of changes to committed terms.
name: External security commitments

evidence.name: Published security, availability and privacy commitments
Check that the commitments match actual practice

description: Breach-notification commitments made in customer contracts are binding and time-bound. If those timeframes are not known to the people running an incident, they will be missed.
implementation_guidance:
Document the breach-notification timeframes committed to customers, including any variation by contract.
Make the shortest applicable commitment the operating standard for the incident process.
Build the customer notification decision into the incident-response plan as an explicit step with an owner.
Maintain current notification contacts for each customer and verify them periodically.
name: Customer breach-notification commitment

evidence.name: Customer contract terms on breach notification
Incident procedure showing the notification timeframes

description: Background screening is the control that applies before trust is extended. Once someone holds production access, the opportunity to verify suitability has already passed.
implementation_guidance:
Run background checks, where legally permitted, before granting access to production or customer data.
Define the check scope by role, applying deeper screening to privileged and finance-facing positions.
Apply the same standard to contractors who receive equivalent access.
Retain evidence that the check was completed and cleared, without retaining unnecessary personal detail.
name: Pre-hire background checks

evidence.name: Background check policy
Completed background checks for a sample of hires

description: Staff are the most frequently targeted attack surface, primarily through phishing and social engineering. Training is the control that turns the workforce from the weakest link into a detection layer.
implementation_guidance:
Deliver security awareness training at onboarding and at least annually thereafter.
Cover phishing, social engineering, credential handling, data classification and incident reporting.
Track completion to 100 percent and escalate non-completion rather than letting it lapse.
Supplement with periodic phishing simulation, using results to target training rather than to penalize.
name: Security awareness training

evidence.name: Training content and schedule
Completion records for all staff

description: Competence is a control-environment criterion, and it starts with defining what a role requires. Where security duties are not written into the role, they are nobody's job in particular.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain role descriptions stating required qualifications, experience and responsibilities.
State the security responsibilities attached to each role explicitly.
Use the description as the basis for the access the role receives.
Review descriptions when roles change materially, and align them with the control ownership map.
name: Job descriptions with security responsibilities

evidence.name: Job descriptions that state security responsibilities

description: Onboarding is the one moment when a new joiner will reliably complete required steps. Agreements, policy acknowledgement, training and correctly scoped access are far harder to collect afterwards.
implementation_guidance:
Use a per-hire checklist covering signed agreements, policy acknowledgement, security training assignment and access request and approval.
Provision access from the role definition rather than by copying another user.
Complete security training within a defined period from the start date.
Record completion per item so onboarding can be evidenced for any individual.
name: Onboarding checklist

evidence.name: Onboarding checklist
Completed checklists for a sample of new joiners

description: Departures are the highest-risk transition in the access lifecycle. Retained access after departure is both a common audit exception and a common breach vector, and ownership of documents and accounts is easily lost with the person.
implementation_guidance:
Use a documented offboarding checklist covering access revocation, device return, credential rotation and transfer of document and account ownership.
Trigger it from the HR system on termination so it cannot be forgotten.
Revoke access within a defined SLA, measured in hours for involuntary departures.
Verify and record completion per item rather than marking the checklist done as a whole.
name: Offboarding and deprovisioning

evidence.name: Offboarding checklist
Completed offboarding records for leavers in the period
Roster of joiners and leavers with dates

description: Confidentiality agreements make the obligation to protect customer and company information legally binding and enforceable, rather than a matter of expectation.
implementation_guidance:
Require a signed confidentiality and intellectual property agreement from every employee and contractor before access is granted.
Ensure obligations survive termination of the engagement.
Track signature status centrally so completeness can be evidenced per person.
Refresh agreements when scope of access or applicable law changes materially.
name: Confidentiality / IP agreements

evidence.name: Confidentiality and IP agreement template
Signed agreements for a sample of staff and contractors

description: Performance management is how competence is maintained rather than assumed. It is where skills gaps, including security-relevant ones, are identified and where accountability for control responsibilities is reinforced.
implementation_guidance:
Run a documented performance evaluation for every employee at least annually.
Assess against clear expectations for the role, including its security responsibilities.
Identify skills gaps and record the resulting training or development actions.
Retain the record of the review, handled confidentially through HR.
name: Performance management

evidence.name: Performance review process
Completed reviews showing control responsibilities were assessed

description: Contractors carry the same access risk as employees but sit outside the HR lifecycle that normally triggers onboarding and offboarding. That gap is where forgotten access accumulates.
implementation_guidance:
Track every contractor in a register with sponsor, scope of access and a mandatory end date.
Apply the same onboarding requirements: agreements, policy acknowledgement, training and approved access.
Trigger deprovisioning automatically from the end date, and require positive action to extend.
Include contractors in access reviews rather than reviewing employees alone.
name: Contractor lifecycle management

evidence.name: Contractor onboarding and offboarding procedure
Contractor register with start and end dates and access

description: Centralizing authentication through one identity provider makes access consistently governed: policy is enforced in one place, and revocation on departure actually reaches every application rather than the ones somebody remembered.
implementation_guidance:
Route access to every system that supports SAML or OIDC through the identity provider.
Enforce MFA, session and password policy centrally at the provider so applications inherit them.
Maintain a documented list of systems that cannot support SSO, with compensating controls for each.
Verify that deprovisioning at the provider removes application access, and check the exceptions explicitly.
name: Enforce single sign-on

evidence.name: Approved exceptions for applications outside single sign on

description: Passwords alone fail against phishing, reuse and credential-stuffing, and stolen credentials remain the most common initial access vector. Multi-factor authentication is the single highest-value access control available.
implementation_guidance:
Require MFA for all users on all systems that support it, with no standing exclusions.
Require phishing-resistant factors such as WebAuthn or hardware keys for administrators and for access to production.
Prioritize systems holding sensitive data and systems controlling network, infrastructure or production if a phased rollout is unavoidable.
Monitor for accounts that bypass or disable MFA, and treat enrolment gaps as findings.
name: Enforce multi-factor authentication

evidence.name: Access policy requiring multi factor authentication
Approved exceptions to multi factor authentication

description: Password policy is the baseline that protects accounts where stronger factors are unavailable. Modern guidance favours length and breach-checking over forced rotation and complexity rules, which drive predictable, weaker passwords.
implementation_guidance:
Enforce the policy centrally at the identity provider rather than per application.
Set a minimum length of at least 12 characters and screen new passwords against known breach corpora.
Avoid mandatory periodic rotation unless a credential is known or suspected to be compromised.
Enforce lockout or rate limiting on repeated failed authentication attempts.
name: Password policy

evidence.name: Password policy

description: Some credentials cannot be replaced by single sign-on, and those are exactly the ones that end up in spreadsheets, chat messages and browser profiles. A managed password manager gives them a controlled home with auditable sharing.
implementation_guidance:
Provide a company password manager and require its use for all shared and non-SSO credentials.
Organize secrets into vaults scoped by team and role rather than one shared vault.
Prohibit credential sharing over chat or email in the acceptable use policy.
Revoke vault access at offboarding, and rotate any shared credential the departing person could read.
name: Company password manager

evidence.name: Policy requiring a password manager for shared credentials

description: Granting access per person produces entitlements nobody can reason about. Defining access by role makes least privilege reviewable, repeatable, and correct by default when someone joins or changes job.
implementation_guidance:
Define roles or groups that map to job functions, and grant access to roles rather than to individuals.
Base each role on the minimum access the function requires, and document what that is.
Provision new joiners from the role definition instead of copying an existing user's access.
Review role definitions periodically, as roles accumulate permissions the same way individuals do.
name: Role-based access and least privilege

evidence.name: Role and access matrix
Role definitions approved by their owners

description: Access granted without a recorded authorization cannot be shown to be appropriate, and it is the point at which least privilege is either enforced or quietly abandoned. The approval record is what an auditor samples to test the control.
implementation_guidance:
Require a documented request and approval before any account or entitlement is created.
Route approval to the system or data owner rather than to the requester's manager alone for privileged access.
Capture the business justification, so the grant can be re-evaluated at the next access review.
Provision only after approval is recorded, and reject retrospective approvals as a matter of process.
name: Access provisioning approval

evidence.name: Access request and approval procedure
Approved requests for a sample of new access

description: The window between someone losing authorization and losing access is a window of unmonitored risk. Departures are also when access is most likely to be used inappropriately.
implementation_guidance:
Trigger deprovisioning automatically from the HR or identity system on termination or role change.
Define an SLA measured in hours for revoking access on involuntary termination.
Cover systems outside SSO, shared credentials, VPN, code repositories and physical access.
Reconcile active accounts against active staff periodically, and investigate every account without a current owner.
name: Timely access removal

evidence.name: Access removal procedure with the timeframe
Removal records for a sample of leavers

description: Access accumulates. People change roles, projects end and temporary grants become permanent, so entitlements that were appropriate when issued drift out of alignment with duties. Periodic recertification is what corrects that drift.
implementation_guidance:
Run access reviews at least annually, and quarterly for production, financial and administrative systems.
Have the system or data owner certify each user individually rather than approving a list in bulk.
Revoke access that is not affirmatively certified, and verify the revocation actually executed.
Retain the review record, the decisions and the evidence of resulting changes.
name: Periodic user access reviews

evidence.name: Access review procedure
Completed access reviews with reviewer sign off
Access changes made as a result of the review

description: Administrative and root access can disable controls, read all data and erase its own traces. It therefore warrants tighter provisioning, shorter tenure and closer review than standard access.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain an inventory of privileged accounts across every system, including cloud root and break-glass accounts.
Require explicit, separately recorded approval for privileged grants.
Prefer just-in-time elevation over standing administrative rights, and log every elevation.
Review privileged access quarterly, and secure break-glass credentials with monitored, alerting access.
name: Privileged access management

evidence.name: List of privileged accounts with approval and need
Review of privileged access

description: Where one person can initiate, approve and execute the same sensitive action, both fraud and simple error go undetected. Separating those duties introduces a second pair of eyes at the point where it matters.
implementation_guidance:
Identify conflicting duty pairs, such as deploying to production and approving that deployment, or creating a vendor and approving its payment.
Separate them in system permissions rather than by convention.
Where team size makes separation impractical, document a compensating control such as independent after-the-fact review of a logged action.
Re-examine separation whenever the team grows or restructures.
name: Segregation of duties

evidence.name: Matrix of conflicting duties
Review of people who hold conflicting access

description: Service accounts, API keys and tokens authenticate without a human present. They are rarely reviewed, frequently over-permissioned, and often outlive the integration that created them.
implementation_guidance:
Inventory every service account, API key and integration token with its owner, purpose and permissions.
Scope each to least privilege, and never use a provider's default or highly privileged service account.
Rotate credentials on a defined schedule and immediately on suspected exposure.
Review the inventory at least annually and disable accounts with no recent authentication activity.
name: Service and machine account governance

evidence.name: Inventory of service accounts and keys with owners
Records of rotation or review

description: Sessions that never expire turn a single stolen laptop or hijacked token into indefinite access. Session limits bound how long a compromised session remains useful.
implementation_guidance:
Configure idle and absolute session timeouts centrally at the identity provider.
Set shorter timeouts for administrative interfaces and systems holding sensitive data.
Require re-authentication for high-risk actions such as changing MFA settings or granting access.
Ensure logout and deprovisioning invalidate active sessions and refresh tokens, not only future logins.
name: Session timeout and management

evidence.name: Session timeout standard

description: Encryption at rest protects data when the storage layer is exposed through a lost device, a misconfigured snapshot, a decommissioned disk or direct access to the underlying store. It is a baseline expectation for confidential and personal data.
implementation_guidance:
Enable encryption at rest on every data store, including databases, object storage, snapshots, backups and disks.
Use platform-managed keys as the minimum, and customer-managed keys where required by commitment or regulation.
Verify encryption is actually enabled rather than assumed, and monitor for unencrypted resources being created.
Ensure new resources inherit encryption by default through policy or infrastructure as code.
name: Encryption at rest

evidence.name: Encryption standard stating what is encrypted and how

description: Data crossing a network can be intercepted or modified in transit. Transport encryption makes intercepted traffic unusable and authenticates the endpoint being connected to.
implementation_guidance:
Enforce TLS 1.2 or higher on all external endpoints, and disable legacy protocols and weak cipher suites.
Redirect HTTP to HTTPS and enable HSTS so downgrade is not possible.
Require TLS for internal service-to-service traffic and for database connections, not only at the edge.
Monitor certificate expiry and automate renewal so an outage does not create pressure to disable TLS.
name: Encryption in transit (TLS)

evidence.name: Encryption in transit standard

description: Encryption reduces to key management. If keys are unprotected, over-shared or never rotated, the encryption they support provides far less assurance than it appears to.
implementation_guidance:
Manage keys in a dedicated KMS or HSM, held separately from the data they protect.
Restrict key use and administration through policy, and separate those two permissions.
Enable rotation on a defined schedule, and define a rotation procedure for compromise.
Log and monitor key use, particularly decrypt operations at unusual volume.
name: Encryption key management

evidence.name: Key management policy
Review of who can use and manage keys
Key rotation records

description: Credentials committed to source code, images or configuration are harvested at scale, and they remain valid long after the commit is reverted. Secrets need a managed store with access control and an audit trail.
implementation_guidance:
Store secrets in a dedicated secrets manager or vault, and never in source control, images or environment files in a repository.
Inject secrets at runtime rather than baking them into build artifacts.
Restrict and log access to each secret, and scope access per service.
Rotate any secret on exposure and on a defined schedule, and treat exposure as an incident.
name: Secrets management

evidence.name: Secrets management standard

description: Flat networks let one compromised host reach everything. Segmentation limits blast radius and keeps data stores off paths that never needed to reach them.
implementation_guidance:
Place databases and internal services in private subnets with no route from the internet.
Define trust zones and control traffic between them with default-deny rules.
Separate production from development and corporate networks.
Verify segmentation by testing reachability rather than by reading the intended design.
name: Network segmentation

evidence.name: Network diagram showing segments and allowed paths
Review of the rules between segments

description: A default-allow network is an inventory problem disguised as a security problem: nobody can enumerate what is reachable. Default-deny inverts that, so exposure is deliberate and documented.
implementation_guidance:
Configure firewalls and security groups to deny inbound traffic by default and allow only what is explicitly required.
Review rules for 0.0.0.0/0 on sensitive ports, and justify or remove each occurrence.
Attach an owner and a purpose to every allow rule so stale rules can be identified.
Review rule sets periodically and remove rules for decommissioned services.
name: Default-deny firewall rules

evidence.name: Firewall rule register with owner and purpose for each rule
Periodic review of firewall rules

description: Internet-exposed SSH and RDP are scanned continuously and are a recurring high-severity finding. Management interfaces should never be directly reachable from the public internet.
implementation_guidance:
Block SSH, RDP and database ports from the internet at the security group and firewall level.
Provide access through a VPN, zero-trust proxy, bastion host or a session manager service instead.
Scan the external surface regularly to detect newly exposed management ports.
Alert on any change that opens a management port to a public range.
name: No management ports exposed to the internet

evidence.name: Approved exceptions for exposed management access

description: Public services face automated attack traffic continuously. A web application firewall filters common injection and scripting attacks, and upstream DDoS protection absorbs volumetric traffic that would otherwise exhaust capacity.
implementation_guidance:
Front public services with a WAF and DDoS protection such as Cloudflare or AWS WAF and Shield.
Start rules in detection mode, tune out false positives, then enforce.
Ensure the origin cannot be reached directly, bypassing the WAF.
Monitor blocked traffic for genuine attack patterns and feed them into detection.
name: WAF and DDoS protection

evidence.name: Review of web application firewall rules and alerts

description: Trusting a device because it sits on the corporate network fails the moment that network includes home offices, contractors and personal devices. Access decisions should rest on verified identity and device posture, not location.
implementation_guidance:
Require a VPN or zero-trust access solution with MFA for administrative access to infrastructure.
Base access decisions on user identity and device posture rather than source network alone.
Grant access per application rather than issuing broad network access.
Log access sessions and review them alongside privileged access.
name: VPN / zero-trust remote access

evidence.name: Remote access standard

description: Cloud workloads are attacked through the control plane as well as the host: credential misuse, cryptomining, anomalous API calls and public exposure. Detection has to cover that plane, not just the operating system.
implementation_guidance:
Enable a managed threat-detection service such as GuardDuty, Defender for Cloud or Security Command Center across all accounts and regions.
Route findings into the on-call and incident process rather than a dashboard nobody watches.
Tune out known-benign findings deliberately, and record the tuning decisions.
Alert on detection being disabled or on an account being created without it.
name: Infrastructure threat detection

evidence.name: Procedure for responding to threat detection alerts
Sample of alerts that were investigated

description: Default configurations are built for compatibility, not security. A hardening baseline replaces those defaults with a known-good standard and gives drift something measurable to be measured against.
implementation_guidance:
Apply CIS Benchmarks or an equivalent hardening standard to operating systems, containers and cloud services.
Build baselines into images and infrastructure as code so new systems start hardened.
Document and approve any deviation from the baseline, with the reason.
Check for drift on a schedule and remediate regressions.
name: Hardening baselines (CIS)

evidence.name: Hardening standard such as CIS or equivalent
Approved exceptions to the standard

description: Full-disk encryption is what makes a lost or stolen laptop a hardware loss rather than a data breach, and it is what allows devices to be disposed of without forensic erasure.
implementation_guidance:
Enforce full-disk encryption on all endpoints through MDM policy.
Escrow recovery keys centrally so encrypted devices remain recoverable.
Report compliance from MDM and remediate devices found unencrypted.
Verify encryption before issuing a device and again during periodic compliance checks.
name: Endpoint full-disk encryption

evidence.name: Endpoint encryption policy
Approved exceptions

description: Endpoints are the most common entry point for malware and the device where credentials and data are most exposed. Detection needs to run on the endpoint itself, where the behaviour occurs.
implementation_guidance:
Deploy endpoint detection and response or anti-malware to every managed endpoint and server.
Enable automatic signature and agent updates.
Monitor agent health and coverage, and treat a device without a healthy agent as an exception to be resolved.
Route detections into the incident process rather than leaving them in a product console.
name: Endpoint EDR / anti-malware

evidence.name: Endpoint protection standard
Alerts that were reviewed and acted on

description: Device management is what makes endpoint controls verifiable rather than advisory. It enforces encryption, patching and screen lock consistently, and provides the remote lock and wipe capability that limits the impact of a lost device.
implementation_guidance:
Enrol all company endpoints in MDM before issuing them to staff.
Enforce baseline policy centrally: encryption, screen lock, patch level and permitted software.
Reconcile enrolled devices against the employee roster to find unmanaged devices.
Define how personally owned devices are handled, either enrolled or denied access to company data.
name: Device management (MDM) enrollment

evidence.name: Device management policy
Inventory of company devices

description: Most successful attacks exploit vulnerabilities for which a patch already exists. Timely patching is therefore among the highest-value controls, and it is one of the easiest to let slip.
implementation_guidance:
Define patch SLAs by severity for operating systems, browsers and installed software.
Automate deployment through MDM or a patch management tool rather than relying on user action.
Report compliance against the SLA and follow up devices that fall behind.
Handle critical out-of-band patches through the emergency change path.
name: Patch management

evidence.name: Patch management policy with timeframes
Patch compliance report

description: A device that leaves the organization with a departing employee, or is lost, still holds company data and cached credentials. Remote wipe is what closes that exposure when the device cannot be recovered.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain remote wipe capability through MDM on all managed devices.
Issue a wipe for lost or stolen devices and for departing employees who do not return hardware.
Confirm the wipe executed rather than assuming the command succeeded, and retain the confirmation.
Cover the case of a device that never reconnects, by rotating credentials it held.
name: Remote wipe on offboarding / loss

evidence.name: Procedure for lost devices and offboarding
Wipe confirmations for recovered or lost devices

description: An unlocked, unattended device grants full access to whoever is nearby, bypassing every authentication control behind it. Automatic locking is what makes physical proximity insufficient.
implementation_guidance:
Enforce automatic screen lock through MDM policy rather than user preference.
Set a short idle timeout, typically no more than 15 minutes, and require authentication to unlock.
Apply the policy to all device types that access company data.
Report compliance and remediate devices that fall out of policy.
name: Screen lock policy

evidence.name: Screen lock standard

description: Confidential data cannot be protected consistently until it has been identified and labelled. Classification is what lets handling rules, access decisions and retention be applied by rule rather than by individual judgement.
implementation_guidance:
Adopt a classification scheme such as public, internal, confidential and restricted.
Define handling rules per level covering storage, transmission, sharing and disposal.
Classify data stores and repositories, not only individual documents.
Train staff on the scheme and reference it in the acceptable use policy.
name: Data classification policy

evidence.name: Data classification policy
Classification applied to systems and data stores

description: Data protection begins with knowing what data exists and where it lives. An inventory that is incomplete guarantees that some data is protected by nobody, because nobody knows it is there.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a data map covering databases, object storage, file shares, analytics platforms and vendor systems.
Record for each store the data categories held, classification, owner, location and retention period.
Note the protections applied to each store, such as encryption, access model and backup treatment.
Refresh the map at least annually and when new systems or vendors are introduced.
name: Data inventory and data map

evidence.name: Data inventory and data map
Review that the inventory is complete

description: Data kept beyond its purpose is pure liability: it expands breach impact, deletion obligations and storage cost without serving the business. Retention that is defined but not enforced technically is retention in name only.
implementation_guidance:
Define a retention period for each data type, based on purpose and legal requirement.
Enforce retention technically through lifecycle rules, TTLs or scheduled purge jobs rather than by manual review.
Apply retention to backups, archives and analytics copies, not only primary stores.
Document any legal hold that suspends normal retention, and lift it when the hold ends.
name: Data retention schedule

evidence.name: Data retention schedule
Evidence data was deleted when retention ended

description: Deletion is only meaningful if the data is actually unrecoverable. Data routinely survives in search indexes, caches, analytics warehouses, vendor systems and backups long after it was deleted from the primary store.
implementation_guidance:
Define a disposal procedure covering primary stores, replicas, search indexes, caches, analytics copies and vendor systems.
Use the data map as the checklist so no store is missed.
Age deleted data out of backups within the documented backup retention window, and state that window in the response to the subject.
Retain a record of what was disposed of, when, and by which method.
name: Secure data disposal

evidence.name: Secure disposal procedure
Disposal records or certificates

description: Copying production data into development or staging silently extends the confidentiality boundary to environments with weaker access control, less monitoring and broader developer access. It is a frequent and avoidable exception.
implementation_guidance:
Populate lower environments with masked, synthetic or subset data rather than production copies.
Prohibit production data in lower environments in policy, and make the approved seeding path the easy one.
Scan lower environments periodically for data that looks like production personal information.
Where a production restore is genuinely required, require approval, time-box it and record the justification.
name: No production data in lower environments

evidence.name: Policy against production data in lower environments
Evidence test data is masked or synthetic

description: The privacy notice is the commitment against which every other privacy control is judged. Where it describes practices that differ from what the systems actually do, the gap is a finding regardless of how strong the controls are.
implementation_guidance:
Publish a privacy notice covering what is collected, why, the legal basis, who it is shared with, how long it is kept and what rights subjects hold.
Write it to match actual data flows, verified against the data map rather than drafted from a template.
Version and date the notice, and retain prior versions.
Notify subjects of material changes through the channel the notice commits to.
name: Privacy notice

evidence.name: Current privacy notice
Notice change history and how data subjects were told

description: Where processing relies on consent, that consent must be freely given, recorded, and as easy to withdraw as it was to give. Consent that cannot be evidenced is equivalent to no consent at all.
implementation_guidance:
Capture consent granularly per purpose rather than as a single blanket agreement.
Store a consent record with timestamp, version of the notice shown, and the method of capture.
Obtain explicit consent where sensitive categories of data are involved.
Honour withdrawal promptly and propagate it to downstream systems and processors.
name: Consent and choice management

evidence.name: Consent records showing when, what and which notice version
Consent withdrawal process and records

description: Data that is never collected cannot be breached, misused or subject to a deletion request. Minimization is the cheapest privacy control available and the one most often skipped.
implementation_guidance:
Map each collection point to the stated purpose it serves, and remove fields that serve none.
Challenge new fields at design review rather than after they are in production.
Keep personal information out of logs, error trackers and analytics events.
Review collected fields periodically and retire those no longer used.
name: Data minimization

evidence.name: Review of each collection point against what is needed

description: Personal information collected for one purpose being used for another is one of the most common privacy failures, and it now arises most often when data is repurposed for analytics or model training.
implementation_guidance:
Restrict access to personal information to roles whose purpose requires it.
Require documented approval before any secondary use, and check it against the purposes disclosed in the notice.
State the position on using customer or personal data for AI and model training explicitly, and enforce it technically.
Review actual data flows against stated purposes at least annually.
name: Limit personal-information use to purpose

evidence.name: Register of the purposes personal information is used for
Review of new uses against the stated purposes

description: Data subjects have the right to access their personal information and, in many regimes, an accounting of who it was disclosed to. These requests carry statutory deadlines and are answered from systems that were rarely designed to answer them.
implementation_guidance:
Operate a documented process with a single intake point and a defined SLA aligned to the applicable regime.
Verify the requester's identity proportionately before disclosing anything.
Compile the response across all systems holding the subject's data, using the data map as the checklist.
Log every request, the response given and the date, so timeliness can be evidenced.
name: Data-subject access request process

evidence.name: Access request procedure
Log of requests with dates and outcomes
Sample responses that include disclosure accounting

description: Data subjects have the right to have inaccurate personal information corrected, and the privacy criteria also require that personal information is maintained accurately for its purpose. A correction that does not propagate leaves the error in place downstream.
implementation_guidance:
Provide a documented path for subjects to request correction of their personal information.
Verify identity before acting on a correction request.
Propagate corrections to downstream systems, processors and backups within a defined window.
Reconcile personal information across systems periodically to detect divergence.
name: Personal-information correction

evidence.name: Correction procedure
Log of corrections and how third parties were told

description: Personal information may only be disclosed to third parties consistently with the notice given and the consent obtained. Without a record of disclosures, neither commitment can be demonstrated, and subject requests for an accounting of disclosures cannot be answered.
implementation_guidance:
Route every new third-party data flow through the vendor review and approval process.
Maintain a disclosure register recording the recipient, data categories, purpose and legal basis.
Verify that each disclosure is consistent with the privacy notice and any consent obtained.
Review the register at least annually against systems actually sending data.
name: Authorized-disclosure governance

evidence.name: Register of authorized disclosures to third parties
Consent or lawful basis for each disclosure

description: The privacy criteria require a record of unauthorized disclosures, not only of incidents that met a notification threshold. Near misses and contained events carry the analysis that prevents the next one.
implementation_guidance:
Record every privacy incident and near miss in the incident register, including those judged not notifiable.
Capture the data categories affected, the number of subjects, the root cause and the containment action.
Record the notification decision and its rationale, including decisions not to notify.
Review the register periodically for patterns rather than treating entries as closed items.
name: Unauthorized-disclosure recordkeeping

evidence.name: Register of unauthorized disclosures including near misses

description: Privacy commitments do not stop at the organizational boundary. Where a vendor processes personal information on your behalf, a data processing agreement is what makes your obligations binding on them.
implementation_guidance:
Execute a data processing agreement with every vendor that processes personal information.
Ensure the agreement covers permitted purposes, security obligations, subprocessing, breach notification, deletion and audit rights.
Track DPA coverage as a completeness metric against the vendor register.
Re-paper agreements when the vendor relationship or applicable regime changes.
name: Data processing agreements with vendors

evidence.name: Executed data processing agreements for vendors that handle personal information

description: Your own breach-notification deadlines start when you become aware of an incident. If a vendor is not contractually obliged to tell you promptly, their delay consumes your statutory window.
implementation_guidance:
Require a breach-notification clause with a specific timeframe, expressed in hours, in every data processing agreement.
Specify what the notification must contain, so the first message is actionable rather than a holding statement.
Record the notification terms per vendor in the vendor register.
Test the contact path for critical vendors, and confirm the notification route is current at review.
name: Vendor breach-notification terms

evidence.name: Vendor contract terms with the breach notification timeframe
Record of vendor notifications received and acted on

description: Breach notification is time-bound by law and by contract, often within 72 hours. Those deadlines cannot be met if the criteria, recipients and templates are decided while an incident is running.
implementation_guidance:
Define the criteria that make an incident notifiable, separately for regulators, customers and data subjects.
Maintain a jurisdiction matrix covering each applicable regime and its deadline.
Pre-approve notification templates with legal so drafting is not on the critical path.
Build the notification decision into the incident-response plan as an explicit step with an owner.
name: Breach notification process

evidence.name: Breach notification procedure and templates
Notification decisions for each incident, including decisions not to notify

description: The privacy criteria require a defined channel for inquiries, complaints and disputes, and evidence that they are addressed. An unmonitored privacy inbox fails the control even where no complaint is ever missed.
implementation_guidance:
Publish a privacy contact point in the privacy notice and on the website.
Route it into a tracked queue with an owner and a response SLA rather than an individual's mailbox.
Record each inquiry, the resolution and the date closed.
Review privacy complaints periodically for systemic causes.
name: Privacy inquiry and complaint handling

evidence.name: Privacy inquiry and complaint procedure
Log of inquiries with resolution times

description: Peer review catches defects and security weaknesses before they reach production and spreads knowledge across the team. Enforced through branch protection, it also produces the authorization trail the change criterion expects.
implementation_guidance:
Require a pull request with at least one approving review from someone other than the author.
Enforce it through branch protection, and disable direct pushes to protected branches.
Require status checks to pass before merge, and prohibit self-approval.
Record any use of an administrator override and review those occurrences.
name: Peer code review (branch protection)

evidence.name: Peer review standard in the development policy
Sample of reviewed changes

description: Automated tests running as a merge gate catch defects while they are cheap and provide repeatable evidence that processing logic behaves as specified. Tests that can be skipped provide neither.
implementation_guidance:
Run the automated test suite on every pull request and require it to pass before merge.
Enforce the gate through branch protection so it cannot be bypassed by individual choice.
Include tests that validate processing accuracy and completeness where the system processes customer data.
Retain build results, as they are the operating evidence that the gate ran.
name: Automated testing in CI

evidence.name: Testing standard stating what must pass before merge
Test run results for a sample of changes

description: Testing in production exposes customer data to unreleased code and makes it impossible to distinguish deliberate change from experiment. Separate environments give changes somewhere to be validated before they carry real consequences.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain distinct development, staging and production environments with separate credentials and accounts.
Promote changes through environments in a controlled sequence rather than deploying directly to production.
Restrict production access to those who require it, and grant lower-environment access more freely.
Keep production data out of lower environments, using masked or synthetic data instead.
name: Separate dev/staging/production

evidence.name: Environment architecture showing separation

description: Unauthorized change is the most common cause of both outages and security regressions. Requiring changes to be authorized, tested and approved before they reach production is the core of the change-management criterion.
implementation_guidance:
Require every production change to carry a recorded authorization and approval before deployment.
Apply the same requirement to database migrations, configuration and infrastructure changes, not only application code.
Link the deployment to the approved change record so the two can be reconciled at audit.
Detect and investigate deployments that reach production without a corresponding approval.
name: Change authorization and approval

evidence.name: Change management policy
Change requests with approval for a sample of changes

description: Emergencies will bypass the normal path, and a process that pretends otherwise simply goes unfollowed. A defined emergency route keeps the control intact by making the bypass explicit, bounded and reviewed.
implementation_guidance:
Define who may authorize an emergency change and under what circumstances.
Require the reason and the actions taken to be recorded at the time, even if briefly.
Require retrospective review and approval within a defined window, normally the next business day.
Review emergency changes at management review, as a rising rate signals a problem with the normal path.
name: Emergency change procedure

evidence.name: Emergency change procedure
Emergency changes with their after the fact review

description: A documented development lifecycle is how security requirements become routine engineering practice rather than individual habit. It also gives new engineers a defined standard to work to, which is what keeps quality stable as a team grows.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a secure development policy covering design review, code review, testing, environment use and deployment.
Include security requirements such as secure coding standards, dependency management and secrets handling.
Define how changes are approved and released, and how emergency changes are handled.
Review the policy annually and align it with the tooling actually in use.
name: Secure SDLC policy

evidence.name: Secure development lifecycle policy
Evidence security was considered in the lifecycle such as design reviews

description: Code that passed review and testing still has to reach production by a path someone controls. A deployment that runs from an unreviewed branch, a laptop or a shared credential bypasses every control upstream, and leaves no record of who released what.
implementation_guidance:
Deploy to production only from the protected default branch or from a release the pipeline built.
Require an approval, or a protected environment with named reviewers, before a production deployment runs.
Limit who and what can deploy to production, and keep deployment credentials in the pipeline rather than on laptops.
Keep the deployment history: what was released, from which commit, when and by whom.
name: Controlled production deployments

evidence.name: Deployment procedure stating who may release to production
Deployment history for a sample of releases showing commit, approver and time

description: An auditor samples changes and asks to see the request, the approval, the review, the test result and the release for each. Where those live in different tools with no link between them, every sample becomes a manual hunt, and a gap in the trail looks like an unauthorized change.
implementation_guidance:
Require every production change to reference a ticket, issue or change request.
Link pull requests to that ticket, and the deployment to the pull request or commit.
Record the approver on the ticket or the pull request, and keep both for the audit window.
Sample changes each quarter and confirm each can be followed from request to release.
name: Change traceability

evidence.name: Change records linking request, review and release for a sample of changes

description: Most application code is third-party dependency code, and vulnerabilities in it are disclosed continuously. Without automated scanning the first notice of an exposed dependency is usually an external report.
implementation_guidance:
Enable dependency and container image scanning on every repository and registry.
Fail builds on newly introduced critical vulnerabilities rather than only reporting them.
Triage alerts to a severity-based SLA and track remediation to closure.
Maintain a software bill of materials so exposure to a new disclosure can be assessed quickly.
name: Dependency and image scanning

evidence.name: Dependency vulnerability triage standard with timeframes
Open alerts triaged within the timeframe

description: A secret committed to a repository should be treated as public from that moment: history is cloned, forked and mirrored, and reverting the commit does not invalidate the credential.
implementation_guidance:
Enable secret scanning on all repositories, including full commit history.
Add pre-commit hooks so secrets are caught before they are pushed.
Rotate any exposed secret immediately, and treat the exposure as an incident.
Investigate whether the exposed credential was used before rotation, rather than assuming it was not.
name: Secret scanning

evidence.name: Procedure for rotating exposed secrets
Records of exposed secrets that were rotated

description: Processing integrity depends on what is allowed into the system. Validating at ingestion keeps malformed, duplicate and out-of-range data from propagating into stores and reports where it is far more expensive to correct.
implementation_guidance:
Validate inputs at the boundary against schema, type, range and required fields.
Detect and handle duplicate submissions explicitly rather than relying on downstream deduplication.
Reject invalid records to a monitored queue rather than discarding them silently.
Alert on rejection rates that exceed expected thresholds, as they indicate an upstream defect.
name: Input validation controls

evidence.name: Input validation standard
Evidence validation was tested

description: Processing can only be tested for correctness against a stated specification. Where behaviour is defined only by the code, there is no independent standard to test against and no basis for an accuracy commitment.
implementation_guidance:
Document data definitions, field-level semantics, calculation logic and processing SLAs.
Version the specification alongside the system so the two do not diverge.
Reference the specification in test cases so tests verify the spec rather than current behaviour.
Review it when processing logic changes, and record the approval of the change.
name: Processing specifications

evidence.name: Processing specifications covering inputs, outputs and accuracy
Review of specifications after change

description: Reconciling outputs against inputs is what demonstrates that processing was complete and accurate. A job that reports success while dropping records is invisible without it.
implementation_guidance:
Monitor job execution for success, failure and non-execution, including jobs that silently do not start.
Reconcile record counts and control totals between source and destination for each run.
Alert on breaks and investigate them rather than reprocessing blindly.
Retain reconciliation results, as they are the primary evidence for the processing integrity criteria.
name: Processing reconciliation and monitoring

evidence.name: Reconciliation procedure
Reconciliation results and how exceptions were resolved

description: Where data passes through a multi-stage pipeline, the intermediate stores are part of the processing path. Data lost or silently truncated between stages produces output that is incomplete without any error being raised.
implementation_guidance:
Use durable, versioned storage for intermediate pipeline stages rather than ephemeral local disk.
Apply integrity checks such as checksums or record counts between stages.
Make stages idempotent so a retry cannot duplicate or lose records.
Align retention of intermediate data with the processing specification and the retention schedule.
name: Pipeline storage integrity

evidence.name: Pipeline storage design showing stages and integrity checks
Integrity check results

description: Logs are the raw material for detection, investigation and evidence. If they are scattered, short-lived or absent, an incident cannot be reconstructed and the operating history cannot be shown.
implementation_guidance:
Centralize security-relevant logs, including authentication, authorization, administrative action, and application audit events.
Retain at least twelve months, with recent data immediately searchable.
Protect logs against modification and restrict who can delete them.
Monitor for logging gaps, as a source that stops sending is itself a signal.
name: Centralized logging and retention

evidence.name: Logging and retention standard
Evidence logs are reviewed

description: Controls apply to systems that are known. An incomplete inventory means some portion of the estate is unpatched, unmonitored and unreviewed, and nobody can say which portion.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain an inventory of systems, cloud resources, endpoints and applications with owner and classification.
Collect it automatically from cloud and identity APIs where possible, as manual inventories decay quickly.
Reconcile it against billing, DNS and identity records to find unregistered systems.
Review the inventory periodically and remove decommissioned assets.
name: Asset and system inventory

evidence.name: Asset inventory
Review that the inventory is complete

description: Alerting on everything trains responders to ignore alerts. A small set of high-signal alerts that are consistently acted on detects more than an exhaustive set that is muted.
implementation_guidance:
Alert on a deliberately limited set of high-signal conditions rather than on every anomaly.
Prioritize unauthorized access attempts, unusual authentication patterns, privilege escalation, service unavailability and resource exhaustion.
Route each alert to an owner with a defined response, and remove alerts nobody acts on.
Review alert volume and false-positive rate periodically, and tune deliberately.
name: Security anomaly alerting

evidence.name: Alerting standard
Review of alert tuning

description: Alerts only reduce risk if someone receives them. An unstaffed alerting pipeline produces the appearance of monitoring without the substance, particularly outside working hours.
implementation_guidance:
Operate an on-call rotation with defined coverage, including nights and weekends where commitments require it.
Route security and availability alerts to the rotation through a system that escalates unacknowledged pages.
Define acknowledgement and response time expectations per severity.
Track missed and unacknowledged pages, and review them as a reliability signal.
name: On-call rotation

evidence.name: On call schedule
Escalation policy

description: New vulnerabilities are disclosed continuously against systems that were secure when deployed. A defined cadence of discovery and remediation is what keeps a hardened estate from drifting into exposure.
implementation_guidance:
Scan infrastructure, containers, dependencies and external surface on a defined schedule.
Define remediation SLAs by severity, and measure performance against them.
Track findings to closure with evidence, and require a documented risk acceptance for anything not remediated.
Feed penetration test and bug report findings into the same tracker so all vulnerabilities are managed in one place.
name: Vulnerability management program

evidence.name: Vulnerability management policy with timeframes
Scan reports
Vulnerability register with remediation and accepted risks

description: Cloud configuration changes take effect immediately and can remove a control silently. Detecting drift from the approved baseline is what turns a one-time hardening exercise into a sustained control.
implementation_guidance:
Monitor cloud configuration continuously against a secure baseline.
Alert on high-risk regressions such as public storage exposure, disabled logging or opened management ports.
Define the remediation path for each alert type, and automate reversion where it is safe to do so.
Review recurring drift for a root cause in the provisioning process.
name: Configuration-change detection

evidence.name: Approved configuration baseline
Alerts on drift that were investigated

description: Not every alert is an incident, and the decision between the two is itself a control. Recording that evaluation is what shows events were assessed rather than ignored.
implementation_guidance:
Define severity levels and the criteria that place an event in each.
Triage every security event and record the assessment, including events determined to be benign.
Define escalation paths and response expectations per severity.
Review triage decisions periodically for consistency and for events that were misclassified.
name: Security event evaluation

evidence.name: Event triage procedure
Sample of evaluated events with the decision

description: Incidents are handled under time pressure with incomplete information. A plan written in advance is what makes the response consistent rather than dependent on who happens to be available.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain an incident response plan defining roles, severity levels and the phases of detection, containment, eradication, recovery and lessons learned.
Include internal and external communication steps, with the notification decision as an explicit gate.
Keep contact details, escalation paths and vendor support routes current.
Review the plan annually and after every significant incident.
name: Incident response plan

evidence.name: Incident response plan
Roles and contact list

description: The value of an incident is the learning, and that is only realized if the analysis is written down and the corrective actions are tracked. Postmortem records are also the audit trail for how an incident was handled.
implementation_guidance:
Run a postmortem for every significant incident, focused on contributing causes rather than individual blame.
Record the timeline, impact, root cause and detection gap.
Raise corrective actions with named owners and due dates, and track them to closure.
Retain the record, and review recurring themes across incidents.
name: Incident postmortems with actions

evidence.name: Postmortem for each significant incident
Corrective actions tracked to closure

description: In a period with no incidents, a tabletop exercise is the only operating evidence that the response plan works. It also surfaces the gaps that are otherwise found during a real incident.
implementation_guidance:
Run at least one tabletop exercise annually against a realistic scenario.
Include the people who would actually respond, including engineering, leadership and communications.
Capture what the exercise revealed, particularly gaps in contacts, access and decision authority.
Track resulting actions to closure and retain the record as evidence the plan was exercised.
name: Incident tabletop exercise

evidence.name: Tabletop exercise plan and report
Actions from the exercise

description: Recovery is the part of incident response most often left undefined, and it is where improvisation causes the most damage: partial restores, missed credential rotation and reinfection from an unclean backup.
implementation_guidance:
Define recovery procedures covering restoring from backup, rebuilding compromised systems and rotating affected credentials.
Establish criteria for declaring recovery complete and returning to normal operation.
Verify system integrity before restoring service, so a compromise is not reintroduced.
Record the recovery steps performed in each incident record.
name: Incident recovery procedures

evidence.name: Recovery procedures
Recovery records for incidents

description: Outages, regional failures and destructive incidents will occur. A plan prepared in advance is what allows recovery within committed timeframes instead of improvising while customers are down.
implementation_guidance:
Maintain a business continuity and disaster recovery plan with defined RTO and RPO per critical service.
Identify critical dependencies, including third parties, and document workarounds for each.
Define activation criteria, roles and communication procedures for customers and staff.
Review the plan annually, test it, and update it after significant architectural change.
name: Business continuity / disaster recovery plan

evidence.name: Business continuity and disaster recovery plan
Exercise or test report
